JC053-VERIFY001 — Reconcile Automated Verification with Live User Behavior

Objective

Restore confidence in the engineering verification process.

Repeated Step 3 tickets have reported successful completion while the Engineering Director immediately reproduced visible failures on the canonical runtime.

No additional implementation work is authorized until the verification mismatch is understood.

Canonical review URL

http://127.0.0.1:8768/?#step-03-job-description

Execution context

- Worktree:
/home/bobreap/projects/teachers-net-jobcenter

- Branch:
JOB-CENTER-JC053-wizard-workbench

Problem statement

The canonical runtime continues to exhibit defects that completed tickets reported as corrected.

Observed examples include:

• unjustified paragraph spacing
• ineffective Clear Formatting
• incorrect list indentation and marker placement
• browser-visible behavior differing from automated verification

This is now treated as a verification-system defect rather than another formatting defect.

Required investigation

1. Reproduce the Engineering Director's exact workflow.

Do not substitute synthetic fixtures.

Use:

- live mouse selection
- live keyboard interaction
- real clipboard paste
- Microsoft Word paste
- Google Docs paste
- Indeed paste when available

2. Compare automated verification versus live interaction.

For every operation record:

- browser events
- selection events
- clipboard events
- DOM mutations
- editor HTML
- preview HTML
- computed styles

Explain every behavioral difference.

3. Determine why automation passes while manual testing fails.

Possible causes include:

- programmatic selection differs from mouse selection
- programmatic paste differs from OS clipboard paste
- automation bypasses focus transitions
- synthetic fixtures differ materially from Office clipboard HTML
- browser-control path differs from live browser interaction
- editor event sequence differs
- another evidenced cause

4. Produce a verification matrix.

For each test:

- automated result
- manual result
- identical?
- if not, explain precisely why

5. Recommend the permanent verification standard.

One of the following must become authoritative:

A.
Automation can faithfully reproduce real usage.

or

B.
Certain editor operations require mandatory human visual acceptance.

Do not leave this undefined.

Formatting review

As part of the investigation also classify the remaining formatting defects:

- paragraph spacing
- list indentation
- bullet positioning
- numbered list positioning
- Clear Formatting

State whether each is:

- implementation defect
- CSS defect
- normalization defect
- verification artifact

No speculative implementation

Unless a defect is conclusively identified during the investigation,
do not produce another formatting patch.

Acceptance

The ticket is complete only when:

- the reason for repeated false-positive verification is explained,
- a permanent verification process is established,
- future formatting tickets can rely on that process.

Git

Documentation/process only unless an implementation change is required to prove the diagnosis.

Stop boundary

Do not resume Step 3 implementation until the verification mismatch has been resolved.

## 5. ChatGPT Integration

Directly visible:

- Conversation text and code blocks.
- User-provided file references when the application exposes them.
- Local files already present in the shared filesystem.
- Instructions and context included in the current task.

Requires manual download or explicit transfer:

- ChatGPT-generated downloadable files that are only represented as download links.
- Files generated in another ChatGPT session but not copied into the shared filesystem.
- Google Drive or other cloud artifacts unless an active connector or accessible link is provided.

Uploaded files:

- If the application places them in the shared filesystem, they can be read directly.
- If they are only represented as conversational attachments without a filesystem path, they are not reliably available to shell tools.
- Windows uploads are often accessible under `/mnt/c/Users/...`, but the exact path must be verified.

Generated downloadable artifacts:

- Not reliably accessible automatically.
- The most reliable handoff is for ChatGPT to write the ticket into the conversation or for the user to download it into a known project/hopper location.

## 6. Workflow Comparison

| Workflow | Speed | Reliability | Context | Auditability | Hopper compatibility | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Downloadable ticket → manual download → Codex | Slowest | High once present | Good if complete | Excellent | Excellent | Manual path/download friction |
| B. Ticket directly in chat → Codex copies it | Fast | High | Very good | Good | Good | Copying omissions or formatting loss |
| C. ChatGPT architects → Codex derives implementation | Fastest initially | Medium | Variable | Weak unless documented | Weak unless Codex creates artifacts | Missing scope, acceptance, exclusions, or stop boundaries |
| D. Structured chat ticket + Codex-generated hopper package | Fast | Highest | Highest | Highest | Highest | Requires consistent prompt structure |

## 7. Recommended Workflow

Use workflow D:

```text
ChatGPT defines architecture and bounded execution ticket directly in chat
↓
Codex reads the ticket from the conversation
↓
Codex inspects local authority documents and repository state
↓
Codex executes only the authorized scope
↓
Codex verifies implementation and runtime behavior
↓
Codex writes report, manifest, cycle record, and evidence into hopper
↓
Codex commits and pushes only authorized files
```

Use downloadable files only when the ticket is unusually large, contains binary evidence, or must be preserved as an immutable external artifact.

Workflow C should not be the default for implementation. Codex can infer routine details, but architecture, scope, exclusions, acceptance criteria, and stop conditions should remain explicit.

## 8. Future Prompt Recommendations

ChatGPT prompts should include:

- Ticket ID and objective.
- Explicit implementation or documentation scope.
- Exact repository and worktree.
- Required authority documents.
- Canonical runtime URL.
- Acceptance criteria.
- Verification requirements.
- Explicit exclusions.
- Commit and push requirements.
- Stop boundary.
- Hopper requirement.
- Whether the request is execute, diagnose, inspect-only, or report-only.

For small bounded changes, the best format is:

```text
Ticket:
Objective:
Repository:
Authority:
Change allowed:
Change prohibited:
Verification:
Commit/push:
Hopper:
Stop boundary:
```

For larger work, include the full ticket directly in the conversation and ask Codex to preserve it in the hopper as the source artifact.

Preferred operating model:

- ChatGPT: architecture, product direction, sequencing, and acceptance definition.
- Codex: repository inspection, implementation, verification, documentation, Git, and hopper packaging.
- Google Drive: operational recovery and shared governance references.
- Local repository docs: durable project authority and implementation truth.

CODEX-019fbfe6-A0640
Role: ASSISTANT
Source line: 18110
Timestamp: 2026-08-06T23:25:58.983Z

Text:
Yes. Re-ingesting the entire companion transcript is unnecessary for routine “next ticket” requests and consumes avoidable quota.

A better protocol:

1. Read only the latest 1–3 turns from the companion chat.
2. Search the returned content for the latest `TICKET READY FOR CODEX`.
3. If the ticket body is complete, execute it directly.
4. Read older turns only when:
   - the latest ticket is truncated;
   - the user says context changed;
   - the ticket references earlier evidence not present locally;
   - a contradiction appears.
5. Use local Cursor, Handoff, authority manifests, and contracts for settled project state rather than rereading chat history.

You can make this even faster by ending each ChatGPT handoff with a standardized marker:

```text
CODEX HANDOFF POINTER

Latest ticket:
<ticket title>

Complete ticket body:
YES

Prior context required:
NO

Required local documents:
<paths>

Stop boundary:
<summary>
```

Then “next ticket” becomes a targeted tail-read operation rather than full transcript ingestion. This preserves context while substantially reducing latency and quota use.

Text:
pls update your workflow and durable guidance documents to incorporate this process - no report or ticket cycle required for this prompt:
REPEATED HUMAN-QA FAILURE ESCALATION

If the same visual or behavioral defect has been addressed in two or more
implementation passes, Codex has reported completion, and human QA still
reproduces the defect:

STOP issuing further speculative implementation patches.

Issue a diagnostic ticket that must explicitly audit for conflicting or
overriding implementation authorities, including as applicable:

CSS
- cascade order;
- specificity;
- duplicate selectors;
- later overrides;
- !important;
- media/container-query conflicts;
- native [hidden] semantics overridden by display rules;
- state-dependent selectors;
- stale/legacy/workbench-derived rules.

JavaScript
- duplicate event handlers;
- multiple state owners;
- later render/update calls;
- DOM cloning/reparenting;
- stale cached state;
- duplicate resource/view stores;
- initialization-order conflicts;
- post-load mutation or overwrite;
- obsolete handlers still participating in production behavior.

DOM / rendering
- duplicate controls or markup;
- hidden elements with nonzero rendered geometry;
- expected elements present but collapsed/offscreen/covered;
- wrong DOM instance being inspected;
- computed styles and actual bounding rectangles.

VERIFICATION REQUIREMENT

Success must be confirmed against the final rendered browser result.

For meaningful visual defects, Codex must:
- capture and inspect a screenshot;
- verify computed styles where relevant;
- verify actual element geometry where relevant;
- compare the visible result against the approved design/state.

DOM attributes, state variables, selector existence, or automated assertions
alone are not sufficient to declare PASS when human QA previously contradicted
them.

If the rendered browser and semantic assertions disagree, the ticket remains
FAIL/BLOCKED until the discrepancy is explained.

CODEX-019fbfe6-A1018

Source line: 30266
Timestamp: 2026-08-09T02:46:18.804Z

Text:
The reports are coherent and materially useful. They identify the browser problem as a control-plane failure, not primarily a Chrome or application failure.

Key conclusions:

- `/json/version` and target listing were false readiness signals.
- WSL-to-Windows transport introduced avoidable failure points.
- Stale/frozen tabs could remain discoverable but non-commandable.
- Helper timeouts did not always cancel underlying operations.
- Normal Chrome is stable under controlled Windows-local CDP testing.
- Browser infrastructure success must remain separate from application acceptance and human visual QA.

The strongest recommendations are:

1. Make command-level browser preflight a hard gate.
2. Use the dedicated Chrome profile only.
3. Create a fresh target before restarting Chrome.
4. Restart only the dedicated QA Chrome, and only after command failure.
5. Retry once, then fail closed.
6. Classify browser verification, engineering diagnosis, and human QA separately.
7. Use convergence tickets after repeated failed implementation attempts.
8. Preserve one terminal report per formal objective rather than packaging every experiment.

Important scope distinction:

- Reports 01–02 are specifically about Durable Views browser QA.
- Reports 03–04 provide broader ChatGPT/Codex workflow guidance.
- The Windows-local CDP procedure should not automatically replace the established Job Center MCP/browser procedure unless explicitly adopted for Job Center. It is compatible as an infrastructure principle, but the project-specific browser authority must remain explicit.

I found no major contradiction among the four reports. The main follow-up is operational adoption: consolidate their recommendations into one authoritative shared workflow, then keep project-specific procedures as thin adapters. Avoid maintaining competing copies of the same browser recovery rules.

pls update your durable governance for this guidance: Recommended evidence policy:
Non-responsive functional tickets: one canonical viewport only.
State/count tickets: prefer DOM/runtime assertions plus one screenshot of the decisive state.
Responsive or visual tickets: capture only the explicitly affected breakpoint(s).
Do not capture desktop/tablet/mobile/narrow matrices by default.
Do not inspect or attach screenshots unless visual acceptance is required.
During convergence, use runtime assertions and the smallest discriminating smoke test.
Run the full acceptance suite once after the narrow invariant passes.
Treat browser preflight’s required readiness screenshot as infrastructure evidence, not product evidence.
Never repeat unchanged screenshots or diagnostics after a passing result.
This reduces tool calls, browser operations, evidence storage, and potential image-token usage. It should not weaken acceptance because functional state tickets are proven primarily through runtime assertions; screenshots remain for human-readable proof when materially useful.
The governing ticket should explicitly classify evidence as one of:
FUNCTIONAL — runtime assertions, optional one screenshot
RESPONSIVE — affected breakpoint screenshots only
VISUAL — reference-specific screenshots
DIAGNOSTIC — targeted evidence only, no acceptance matrix
I recommend adding a durable rule:
Responsive screenshot matrices are prohibited unless the ticket explicitly concerns responsive layout, breakpoint behavior, visual convergence, or human visual comparison. Functional and state tickets require only the minimum canonical viewport evidence necessary to prove the requested behavior.

SOURCED-JOB V1 SCHEMA ASSESSMENT:
MINIMAL SCHEMA EVOLUTION REQUIRED

Completed the read-only JC057 architecture audit.

Key findings:

- Existing provenance/import infrastructure is substantial and supports source IDs, requisitions, URLs, observations, hashes, reconciliation, and exceptions.
- No suitable pre-Job discovery/staging entity exists.
- Controlled ingestion currently creates canonical Jobs immediately after validation.
- Employer-level sourcing policy storage does not exist.
- Employer Admin managed-state detection requires the future capability boundary.
- Email transport is partial; Jobs bell notifications and notification queue storage are absent.
- Existing `job_sources` can preserve sourced provenance, but exact provenance values and promotion rules need an authority contract.
- School / Jobsite resolution needs an explicit resolved-resource seam for sourced discoveries.
- Semantic duplicate detection should remain advisory.
- Careers URLs, ATS integrations, Jobsite policy overrides, Recruiter-specific sourcing, and inactivity thresholds remain deferred.
- No code, schema, data, notification, or runtime changes were made.

[Full audit report](</home/bobreap/projects/teachers-net-site/tmp/hopper/jobcenter/Report (Job Center)/jc057-sourced-job-discovery-policy-schema-audit-report-jobcenter-260810150000.txt>)

**Diagnosis**

The previous session failed because its available tool surface did not expose the ChatGPT-backed conversation reader at the moment it tried to refresh the companion chat.

In the current session, `codex_app.list_threads` is available and returns:

- `Job Center (8/10/26)`
- `kind: chatgpt`
- thread ID `6a79d7ea-da44-83e8-91eb-460b99ab593b`
- `unavailableSources: []`

Then `codex_app.read_thread` successfully read the ChatGPT tail and recovered the full `JC053-STEP2-INTEGRATION` ticket.

In the previous attempt, the local Codex transcript shows it repeatedly reported that the ChatGPT connector was unavailable and that only the local Codex transcript was readable. So the failure was not that the chat did not exist, and not that you were naming the wrong session. It was a session/tool-availability problem: that Codex runtime did not have the ChatGPT source exposed when it tried.

There was also a secondary ticket-format issue in the companion ChatGPT chat: ChatGPT had apparently emitted a fenced block with metadata like ` ```text id="..." `. Your durable parser expects a plain ` ```text ` fence with first non-empty line exactly `TICKET READY FOR CODEX`. But that format issue was not the main reason the prior Codex session could not connect. It became relevant only after connection was restored.

**Most likely cause**

The previous Codex turn was operating in a detached/local Codex context with an incomplete or stale app-tool registry. After the context/model transition, `tool_search` surfaced the proper app thread tools, and the app returned ChatGPT threads directly. That is why the same project chat became visible now.

Official OpenAI Codex app-server documentation describes conversation history and stored thread reads as app-server-backed capabilities, so this kind of failure sits in the app/client integration layer rather than the repository or ticket layer: [Codex App Server](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server).

**Process correction**

For future “connect to ChatGPT chat” requests, I should do exactly what worked here:

1. Search/load the thread/chat tool.
2. Run `codex_app.list_threads`.
3. Confirm the target is `kind: chatgpt`, not `kind: codex`.
4. Read only the tail with `codex_app.read_thread`.
5. If ChatGPT is missing or listed unavailable, report “ChatGPT source unavailable” before falling back to asking for pasted ticket text.

The earlier session stopped too soon and over-attributed the problem to ticket format. The cleaner conclusion is: connector unavailable first, ticket fence strictness second.

CODEX-019fbfe6-A1518
Role: ASSISTANT
Source line: 39512
Timestamp: 2026-08-10T22:48:48.530Z

Text:
Yes. The faster path is to bypass the Codex thread-reader entirely and extract directly from the raw JSONL with a narrow allowlist.

The important discovery from the test is this: the renderer itself did not take 8 minutes. The raw 247 MB session rendered in about 12–13 seconds per pass. The long runtime came from the diagnostic ceremony: double render, full SHA passes, thread-reader comparison, report writing, hopper cycling, validation, and my own tool-call overhead.

For routine use, I’d use three modes:

1. Fast tail mode — best for “next ticket”

Read the raw session JSONL from the end in byte blocks, extracting only visible `user` / `assistant` message records until we find the latest complete `TICKET READY FOR CODEX` block.

Expected time: seconds.

No full transcript. No thread-reader. No broad context reload.

2. Fast full-chat mode — best for handoff transcript

Single streaming pass over raw JSONL:

- include only user-visible user messages;
- include only assistant-visible messages;
- exclude system/developer/tool/reasoning/output records;
- preserve timestamps, source line, role, and stable IDs;
- skip full thread-reader comparison unless explicitly auditing completeness.

Expected time for a 247 MB session: roughly 15–30 seconds.

3. Indexed mode — best long-term

Create a compact local sidecar index per Codex session:

```text
session-id.index.jsonl
line_number
byte_offset
timestamp
role
message_id
content_hash
short_preview
```

Then future operations can jump directly to visible messages or the newest ticket without reparsing the 247 MB raw file.

Expected time after index exists: near-instant.

My recommendation:

- For normal ticket retrieval: use fast tail mode.
- For handoff: use fast full-chat mode.
- For fossil-record/audit work: use full diagnostic mode with SHA, double render, credential scan, and comparator.

The key procedural correction is: do not use `read_thread` pagination as the normal extractor. It is useful as a comparator, but it can drag tool payloads, screenshots, and internal event material back into the context window — exactly the stuff we are trying not to load.
